newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana surplus spent improperly, auditor says.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana surplus spent improperly, auditor says.

text.p: Louisiana did not use 1995 surplus dollars as constitutionally required to retire outstanding debt, legislative auditor Dan Kyle said in a disputed report.

The state constitution requires that nonrecurring surplus revenues be used to retire or defease bonds "in addition to existing amortization requirements of the state," Kyle said in a report given to lawmakers Tuesday.
The state had a surplus of $106.6 million for fiscal 1995 and did use about $18 million of that to defease three bond issues in 1995 that were scheduled to be paid out in fiscal 1996.
But the remaining $88 million was used to make regularly scheduled debt service payments in fiscal 1996, Kyle said.

"This had the effect of reducing the state's debt service expenditures paid from current collections, thereby freeing up funds for other purposes. However, this approach did not fulfill the constitutional requirement that the funds be used 'in addition to existing amortization requirements,'" Kyle's report said.
He said the state should have used all the surplus to defease additional bonds in fiscal 1995, and paid 1996 debt service from current collections.

The report comes amid plans to use $318 million of surplus revenues in a similar way this year. Gov. Ken Foster's administration has proposed using $104 million to retire long-term debt and using the rest to make regularly scheduled debt service payments for fiscal 1998.

Kyle had warned in the 1995 annual report, before the surplus from that year was spent, that he considered the proposed use of the money to be "improper." Commissioner of Administration Mark Drennen disagreed, noting that the state attorney general had issued an opinion finding the use of the money "proper and legal in all respects."
Kyle reiterated his claim that the money was spent improperly in his audit for fiscal 1996, which was released Tuesday.

"They're saying if they set that money aside before the end of 1995, that 1996 (payment) is a future year. We say, technically, that is not what the law calls for," Kyle said in a telephone interview Wednesday.

The legislative auditor is a fact-finding body with no regulatory authority, Kyle said. The auditor's office can refer the case to the state attorney if criminal action is suspected. Or it can ask the bipartisan Legislative Audit Advisory Counsel to review the case and seek a judicial ruling.
Kyle said he would do the latter because, "I don't see anything criminal in this."
